name: Dry fasting

lead: Dry fasting means going without both food and water. Studies cover religious daytime fasts such as Ramadan and the Bahá'í fast, plus one small five-day physiology study.
Online advocates cite autophagy and other benefits; these claims have not been tested for appearance.

paras: Without fluids the body faces reduced blood volume and higher solute concentration, triggering hormones such as vasopressin and aldosterone.
Prolonged fasting can cause electrolyte losses and, without fluids, dehydration. Long dry fasts have little formal safety research.

lead: Dry fasting is abstaining from both food and fluids for a period of time. It occurs in religious practice, such as daytime fasts of the Bahá'í Faith and Ramadan, and in some wellness circles that advocate longer dry fasts.[1][2]
Advocates in online communities say it deepens fasting effects such as autophagy. Research on dry fasting is small and mostly examines religious daytime fasts in healthy volunteers.[1][2][3]
Medical sources note that prolonged fasting can cause electrolyte losses, and fluid restriction adds dehydration risk; the entry is classed here as carrying high risk.[4]

paras: Fasting broadly means voluntarily abstaining from food and sometimes drink. Many faiths include fasting: Muslims abstain from dawn to sunset during Ramadan and the Bahá'í Faith observes a nineteen-day fast. These daytime fasts are forms of intermittent dry fasting.[1][3]
A cohort of 34 healthy Bahá'í volunteers was studied during the 19-day daytime dry fast for safety and effects on hydration, metabolism and the circadian clock.[1]

In a small study, ten participants performed dry fasting for five consecutive days with daily monitoring of hormones including ADH, aldosterone and cortisol, to describe the physiological responses to reduced blood volume and increased solute concentration.[5]
A three-arm randomized trial in 16 subjects without diabetes compared Bahá'í dry fasting, time-restricted eating and control on glucose profiles.[2]
A prospective cohort of healthy people examined body composition, inflammatory and mental-health parameters during Ramadan.[3]
Dawn-to-dusk dry fasting studies in people with metabolic syndrome or raised body mass index examined inflammatory cytokines and proteome changes.[6][7]

Wikipedia notes that prolonged fasting can lead to loss of sodium, potassium and magnesium and may cause low blood sodium, muscle loss, gallstones, and refeeding syndrome after about four to five days without food. A 2026 narrative review summarises fasting effects across several body systems.[4]
Medical guidance for fasting generally addresses food abstinence; effects of complete dry fasting beyond daytime fasts have received little formal study.
